item.title: Overcoming Extreme Anxiety: Tips from a Christian Counselor in Texas
item.description:
Anxiety affects millions of people in the United States annually. Extreme anxiety can lead to physical and mental conditions, such as high blood pressure, heart disease, stomach issues, headaches, panic attacks, and unexplained aches and pains.

Extreme anxiety can interfere with your job and relationships. It can keep you from taking action on good opportunities or attending special events. Anxiety can rob you of your confidence and self-esteem.

God created your body to react to stress to protect you from danger and predators. Unfortunately, our minds perceive danger to also include stressful events or late mortgage payments. Other factors, like brain structure or function, brain chemical imbalance, genetics, family history, trauma, or environmental factors, contribute to increased levels of anxiety.

You can learn to control extreme anxiety through lifestyle changes, professional treatment, and support.

Tips for Overcoming Extreme Anxiety

Overcoming extreme anxiety means looking at the condition from all angles. You need an approach that addresses physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual health. If you rely solely on one, you risk neglecting other areas.

For example, if you concentrate on using exercise to fight anxiety and depression without addressing negative thoughts and challenging old beliefs, the thoughts will continue and fuel your anxiety.

Think of your brain like a giant computer. Anxiety is like an open tab running in the background. Perhaps you are not working on that screen currently, but it is still running and consuming power and resources from your computer. Anxiety is like that underlying tab, leaving you feeling worried, on edge, and mentally frazzled.

The following are several tips for overcoming extreme anxiety.

Seek counseling

Counseling provides the opportunity for a safe space to delve into the root of your anxiety, identify anxious thoughts, challenge negative beliefs, and learn how to reframe thoughts to result in positive outcomes.

Talk therapy is most commonly known in counseling, followed by Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). CBT is used widely for various mental conditions. It is based on identifying and analyzing negative thoughts. These anxious thoughts influence emotions and behaviors. By changing the way we think, we increase the likelihood of feeling and acting differently.

Exposure therapy is a method that gradually introduces the client to a situation to assist in the desensitization process. For example, for clients with extreme anxiety in social situations, a counselor may suggest minimal exposure initially. This might look like a short trip to the drugstore to purchase one item or walking into a café to buy a coffee on the least busy day.

Your counselor will customize a plan for your situation and the severity of your anxiety symptoms.

Lower stress

We have all been told to manage stress, but doing it is easier said than done. Engaging in activities that lower stress will activate the parasympathetic nervous system. This lowers adrenaline and cortisol levels, and improves blood pressure and resting heart rate.

You can lower stress right away by practicing deep breathing. When you feel anxious, take a few minutes to inhale through your nose for the count of four, hold the breath for the count of four, then release through the mouth for the count of four. Repeat as necessary. Take note of any tense muscles and try to relax them as you exhale.

To lower stress for the long term, take a look at your schedule and responsibilities. Is there anything you can delegate to others or delete? Are you taking on too much? Have you set unrealistic expectations for yourself? Learn to set boundaries and say no. Prioritize tasks that align with your beliefs and values, and stop striving using your own strength. As we know, our own strength is nothing compared to God’s strength. Let Him lead you.

Make exercise a habit

Exercise lowers stress hormones and releases a flood of endorphins, serotonin, dopamine, and other neurotransmitters. This combination boosts mood, improves cognitive function, strengthens cardiovascular processes, and builds confidence.

To receive the most benefit, make exercise a part of your daily routine. It should become a habit just like brushing your teeth. If you want to make the habit stick, stack the habit onto another well-established one.

For example, stretch for 10 minutes after brushing your teeth in the morning. Or, slip your workout clothes on as soon as you arrive home after work and lift weights for 30 minutes before making dinner. You are more likely to stick with it if it’s part of your regular schedule.

Turn bedtime into a routine

Sleep should be a priority. You will have a harder time regulating emotions if you skimp on sleep. Sleep can also elude you due to anxious thoughts, making it challenging to fall and stay asleep during the night.

Create a bedtime routine to initiate sleep. For example, shower or change into pajamas after dinner to signal to your brain that it is time to unwind. Choose two or three habits you will incorporate into this routine. You could choose to turn off your devices, brew a cup of herbal tea, and read a book before bed. Choose relaxing activities. If you exercise, complete your workout at least three hours before bed, so that the endorphin rush does not interfere with sleep.

Eat healthier food

We have all heard the suggestion to eat healthier food, but we may not realize that nutrition plays a part in mental health. The foods you eat can influence how you feel. Some substances worsen anxiety and depression symptoms. Some ultra-processed foods dull cognitive function, leading to brain fog.

Aim to eat nutritious, balanced meals of lean proteins, healthy fats, complex carbohydrates, and fresh fruits and vegetables. Avoid over-consuming alcohol, caffeine, and sugar. If possible, choose whole foods over packaged items.

Join a support group

A support group for participants struggling with extreme anxiety can provide you with community, structure, encouragement, and advice from others with anxiety disorders. Often led by a counselor, these groups encourage participants to share their struggles and how they have overcome anxiety.

Many support groups engage in activities that bring the group closer. You may role-play or brainstorm solutions to participants’ problems. These sessions are an excellent opportunity to share what has worked for you and to help others.

Consider your inner circle

Toxic friendships and relationships can create extreme anxiety. Consider the relationships you have with those in your inner circle. Is there mutual respect and honor? Is there a form of abuse? If you are in an abusive relationship, seek help immediately.

Remove or limit connections that leave you feeling anxious, drained, or depressed. A counselor can help you shift from these toxic connections to more beneficial ones.

Turn your anxiety over to god

We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not abandoned; struck down, but not destroyed. – 2 Corinthians 4:8-9, NIV

The Bible reminds us that we are never alone. The Lord will never leave us. There will always be trouble. Fear and worries may try to overtake us, but God can give peace that no one understands. Jesus reminds us, “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.” (John 14:1, NIV)

Don’t give up even when extreme anxiety fills your mind with panic. Pray and ask God to bring you peace and joy like no other. Jesus can handle all of your worries, anxious thoughts, and fears. He can handle all of it. Take it off your shoulders and give it to Him. You can overcome extreme anxiety through Him.

Do you need help with extreme anxiety?

If you have experienced episodes of extreme anxiety or panic attacks, contact our Christian counseling center today to speak to a representative. Our center will connect you to a counselor specializing in anxiety disorders, who can facilitate an assessment and help you create a mental health care plan to overcome extreme anxiety using effective psychological methods and Biblically based principles. Call us today for an appointment.

item.title: Five Things That Negatively Impact Male Mental Health the Most
item.description:
Statistically, men are less often diagnosed with depression than women, and yet are more likely to commit suicide. There is something important about male mental health that lurks in the gap between these two facts: that men are seemingly less depressed than women, but take their own lives in far greater numbers every year.

This disparity raises the question: “Why is it that more men are dealing with depression but not talking about it? Why do more men not seek help when they experience depression?”

Many men suffer silently because they simply don’t have the vocabulary to describe their struggle, while others are just trying to get by without having to ask for help. Men have been raised to believe that asking for help is a sign of weakness, or sold lies about masculinity and mental health. However, the truth of God’s Word will ultimately set men free if they can learn to tune into the right “voices” and obtain correct information.

No man wants to feel impotent or victimized, but the truth is that men do struggle. Being a man does not mean being on par with gods and angels. They bleed, they get hurt, life affects them, and it is only when men acknowledge that they’re stuck or struggling that they can find the help they need to heal or move on.

Maybe it’s time to address the shame and fear that have been holding men back, assess the situation they’re in, and talk to each other about the struggle. In this way, men can begin to make progress as men and as individuals by talking privately and openly with a trusted friend, or even accessing the power of a group of men sharing similar experiences.

You are never truly alone unless you want to be. Jesus Himself was an example of not carrying a burden alone. He shared the challenges he faced with His disciples openly and lovingly, and they responded to Him in kind.

Individuals and the Collective

For the most part, men have been taught that vulnerability is a kind of weakness. To be masculine is to be “strong,” and to be “strong” equates to handling life’s difficulties on their own.

From the youngest age, men are taught that boys don’t cry and that any emotion other than anger and apathy is for the weak. Even the milder depictions of masculinity that were modeled were sometimes toxic, if only because they were built on incomplete understandings of male mental health.

Boys do cry, show hurt, sadness, tenderness, and affection, along with the whole range of human emotions. So do men. Men are mentally, emotionally, and physically complex by design, and that is an important and powerful part of God’s design. Besides this, men are all individuals with unique experiences, insights, skills, and traumas.

Only when people begin to understand and accept men as individuals can we begin to figure out where each of us fits into the collective. There might be some broad cultural ideals that men are expected to meet, but we will each reach these goals by taking our own unique paths to them.

The man who uses his hands to build houses in the village is no less valuable than the man who plants crops and flowers, and no less valuable than the disabled man who is only able to tell stories and speak sense to the next generation.

In the same way, men who show more masculine physical traits and/or limited emotional expression could learn from men around them that there are many benefits to softer, more sensitive emotions, which they often avoid. Each man has different roles, unique struggles, personal pressure points, and each of these things determines value as individuals first and as men second.

At the end of the day, each man is responsible for himself, his spouse or partner, and his family. Some men’s greatest achievement in life is that they are patient and kind toward others, and generous and loving toward themselves as well, even while maintaining ordinary jobs and receiving minimum wage.

Five Things That Negatively Impact Male Mental Health

Regardless of your unique skills, personality, or life experiences, as a man, you will face one or more of the following struggles, statistically speaking. Male mental health is affected by a collection of similar struggles that seem to reach across generations and cultures.

These are the things that we must face head-on, be vocal and honest about as we navigate them, and find our way of getting through them to avoid being part of the tragic statistics. Unfortunately, there is no road map or blueprint for how to get through this stuff. Each man must do his best, help his brothers, accept help from those who love him, and keep going.

Unemployment and Work Struggles

The one aspect of life where men draw our worth from the most is our contribution to society. Men know that if we don’t work, we don’t eat; that’s just how the world works. Sadly, life isn’t just as simple as finding a well-paying job and doing that until retirement.

Sometimes it takes decades to find something that they enjoy doing and are good at, and even then, the job market is so unstable that they aren’t guaranteed employment, a healthy work environment, or a manageable workload.

Few things negatively impact male mental health more than unemployment, especially when it lasts for months and years. Criticism and harsh words around this situation can often cut the deepest in a man’s security in a relationship and his self-image.

At the core, men not only need security and stability, but also to know that they are making a valuable contribution somewhere. They need to know that they are seen and appreciated, even as they struggle. It is not weak or shameful to need to feel valued; in fact, it is a sign that they see their own value.

Money Problems

Men work to contribute something valuable, but also to find financial stability. They might not be able to find a job that offers both, but if they can’t at least find a way to put food on the table and pay bills, their mental health will plummet in a sea of anxiety and fear. When there is the added pressure of having a family to provide for, the strain of not making enough money is enough to sink any man’s health.

Relationship Issues

God said right at the start that it wasn’t good for man to be alone. Many men have learned to cope well with being on their own, but for those with marriages and families, nothing is more tumultuous than a family torn apart by divorce or separation.

Male mental health is often at its lowest when there is a dramatic change in the family and a lack of social support through these changes. Regardless of the cause of these struggles, no man can navigate these experiences alone, and some don’t make it through these struggles alive.

Isolation

Men are more likely to try to cope privately and silently with their problems. Many grew up with fathers who were fixers, who never asked for help and who never modeled vulnerability and humility. Male mental health suffers most in stubborn silence and in isolation.

If you find yourself without a decent support system or without people to talk to or listen to your experiences, make changes as soon as possible. Having even a single confidant or trusted friend can make all the difference to male mental health.

Stigma

Perhaps you are trying to navigate life alone because that’s what was expected of you. That is the case for many men. Here’s the thing about stereotypes and toxic masculinity, though: it kills. If you have spent your entire life internalizing your struggles and externalizing your aggression, you have missed out on some of the most fundamental experiences of being a man.

Brotherhood, vulnerability, accountability, and humility are all vital aspects of masculinity, yet many are bound by misguided, cruel, and damaged depictions of manhood. Lies will keep you bound in fear, but the truth will release you to be the best version of yourself possible.

Discover Better Mental Health

If you have never asked for help or opened up about your struggles, this is your challenge to do so. The idea of opening up to someone might fill you with dread, and you might not even have the language to describe what you are going through. Counselors and therapists are impartial, patient, and non-judgmental third parties who provide a safe space in which you can be completely honest.

You can start by consulting our online catalog of counselors, where you will hopefully find someone suitable, or you may ask our reception team to help connect you with someone. You no longer have to struggle alone; there is someone out there who will listen without judgment.

item.title: Children’s Mental Health: Five Toxic Phrases NOT to Say to Your Kids
item.description:
Most parents strive to be loving, supportive, and caring to their children. They read self-help and parenting books to learn how to be the best parents they can be. They painstakingly curate friendships to help their kids thrive and run to the rescue whenever someone says something offensive to them. They may even rehearse pep talks and thoughtfully craft sentimental birthday card messages.

And yet, even the most well-intentioned parents fall short of their own parenting ideals sometimes. In stressful moments, you might not take the time to consider your words. You might repeat phrases you heard growing up that seem to work in specific situations. Other times you might not be mindful of your words at all.

Some clichés and rote statements seem to be inherited as they have been used and reused by parents for generations. And they can creep out of your mouth without much forethought.

They might sound harmless, even motivating, but these common, seemingly benign comments can negatively impact children’s mental health and shape how your children view themselves and their place in the family.

Why can’t you be more like ____?

How does the old saying go: “Comparison is the thief of joy.”

If you’re a parent and you don’t think your child is quite living up to their potential or is making questionable choices, you might be tempted to use peer pressure to motivate them into better choices. You point out the good things you see in others their age as a means of motivation.

To you, you’re showing them a good example of proper behavior. To them, you’re favoring someone else over them. While you might think that you’re motivating your child, you are likely pushing them into envy more than corrective action.

What children hear instead of a motivation speech is the painful message that they’re not enough for you. That you don’t think they’re smart enough or well-behaved or disciplined enough. That you, the one who is supposed to love them unconditionally, prefer another over them.

Your child was uniquely made, and comparing them to others distorts that beautiful truth. Or, as the saying goes, it robs them of their joy and can lead to a lifelong struggle with the insecurity of never being enough.

You’re getting big

What’s wrong with noticing that your child is so much bigger than when they wore that outfit last month? That’s a good thing, right?

Parents may mean, “Look how much you’ve grown,” or “I can’t believe how fast time is going by.” But for children, especially as they become increasingly aware of their bodies, this comment can land differently than intended.

The occasional neutral observation about growth doesn’t cause devastating harm, but repeated evaluation can. Rather than hearing admiration or mere observation, children may hear an evaluation of their size. Even young kids can begin to internalize that having their body monitored, commented on, or judged is normal, and that is not a lesson you want to teach your children.

Western culture is already obsessed with weight and appearance, so comments about a child’s body, no matter how well-intended or casual, can teach them that their value is tied to how they look rather than who they are in Christ.

In addition, when these body comments come from parents, it can normalize them so your child ingests body comments as valid from anyone and everyone, essentially giving an open door for the world to dictate your child’s self-worth based on appearance only.

You ate more than I did

This phrase often slips out without any intention to shame, but as a simple observation or even in jest. But children are keen observers, and comments about how much they eat can quickly turn toxic.

When adults point out portion sizes or compare their own eating habits to a child’s, kids can misinterpret the messaging. While the comment might be thought of as a nonchalant observation to you, it lands as a criticism and comparison to them. This can affect their eating habits and create a toxic relationship with food. Associating food with criticism or shame may contribute to disordered eating patterns.

As their parent, it’s your duty to provide healthy foods and balanced meals. It’s important that you teach your child about good eating habits and to model normal portion sizes. But rather than commenting on how much your child eats, trust that their growing bodies know what they need. And if you have a concern, talk with your child’s pediatrician.

Give them a hug

It can feel pretty awkward for you when your child is in a social situation where a friendly hug might be expected. Meeting distant relatives for the first time, seeing grandparents after a long time apart, or saying goodbye to a friend after a play date may feel like the proper time for an embrace.

If you’re an outgoing, tactile person, you might feel that it’s natural to hug in these social situations. You might even want to encourage your child to be friendly and develop a habit of open affection.

But when you pressure your child to give physical affection that they’re not comfortable with, you aren’t really teaching them how to be openly affectionate. The message that they’re likely receiving is that their personal boundaries are less important than someone else’s feelings or their own social comfort.

Even when the request comes from a safe and familiar adult, like a parent, being told to “just give them a hug” removes a child’s autonomy over their own body. And as they mature, it can make it more difficult for them to recognize when something feels wrong or to speak up when their boundaries are crossed.

As you work on this as a parent, it will be important for you to teach your children how to speak up for themselves in a respectful way when the situation arises. For example, it will be beneficial for you to teach your child to say something like, “I am not ready for a hug right now.” Or, “I can give you a high five.”

Stop crying

For years, society has told children to “stop crying.” On the surface, it’s seen as an attempt to get the child to learn emotional regulation. It’s meant to calm a tense situation. But under those surface-level goals lies a toxic concept.

By telling your children to “stop crying,” you are denying them the right to feel and react authentically. You are dismissing or minimizing their experiences and telling them that their tears need to be stopped so that those around them aren’t uncomfortable.

Healthy emotional regulation is different than silencing emotions. Regulation invites children to acknowledge their feelings and guides them through them. With repeated orders to simply squelch their tears, children will eventually see their emotions as something that must be hidden rather than naturally expressed. And while parents might look at this as emotional regulation, in truth, it’s emotional suppression.

Seeing your child cry is an opportunity to validate feelings, empathize, and teach proper emotional expression. Asking an emotional child questions can teach them to more readily identify why they are emotional in the first place. This will lead to an opportunity for them to actually process a triggering situation and learn from it. Suppressing emotions will eventually lead to negative self-worth.

Godly parenting

The gift of parenthood also comes with responsibility. Many parents like to quote the first part of Ephesians chapter 6, where children are told to obey their parents in the Lord, because it is right. It tells children to “Honor your father and mother”. But the directive doesn’t stop there. The Bible holds both sides responsible for the health of the parent-child relationship.

Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord – Ephesians 6:4, NIV

That verse is key.

Scripture doesn’t give parents unchecked authority as many may think. It places a clear responsibility on them to not provoke and to instruct and discipline with love. Colossians 3:20-21 also tells parents not to embitter their children so they will become discouraged (NIV).

Obedience grows best in a loving and respectful environment, not in the middle of fear and domination. And because of this directive, it’s important to choose your words prayerfully and wisely.

In Matthew 12:36, Jesus says that people will have to give an account for every “idle word” they speak. Idle words aren’t always cruel or even intentional, but they are still damaging. And in parenting, they’re often thoughtless, habitual phrases spoken without a second thought but with great consequence.

Therapy

If you grew up in a household that used these and other toxic phrases, you might use them too. Without forethought or concern for consequences, you just repeat what you’ve been told and what has been modeled for you.

But with maturity and knowledge comes the obligation to do better than you were given. And now you know. You know that these phrases that spill from your mouth out of habit and history are not benign or neutral but are toxic and potentially harmful to your children.

If you need help identifying areas in your own upbringing that are affecting your parenting, please contact our reception team today to schedule an appointment with me or another capable counselor in our online directory.

Together, you and your therapist can rewind your life, identify the areas that left an impression on you, and that are still shaping you as a parent and person.

item.title: Breaking the Cycle: How Family Issues Shape Mental Health Across Generations
item.description:
Family issues have a distinct way of echoing through time. Unresolved conflict, unspoken pain, or unhealthy patterns in one generation likely resurface in the next. The result is the shaping of a generation in how they understand relationships, process emotions, and view themselves. Family dynamics and mental health are connected, as seen in daily interactions. These interactions may be how they respond to stress, or the beliefs they carry about their worth in the future.

Whether it is recognized or not, what gets passed from one generation to the next shows up in real and lasting ways. The weight of those effects can quietly shape how a person sees themselves, how they relate to others, and whether they believe change is even possible. Understanding connection is the first step toward breaking a cycle that no longer serves anyone.

Proverbs instructs people on the importance of showing children good ways of living. “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.” (Proverbs 22:6, NIV) Everyone should consider this to help each generation grow up well.

The Weight of What Gets Passed Down

It’s not just recipes or photo albums that families pass down from previous generations. Unaddressed trauma, patterns of communication, and coping mechanisms are also handed down — often without anyone realizing what is happening. A parent who learned to suppress emotions may raise children who do the same, and a grandparent’s anxiety about finances can create a legacy of scarcity.

These patterns become so familiar that they feel like personality traits rather than learned behaviors. What makes this process difficult is that many of the behaviors are never spoken out loud. They are absorbed through observation, quiet signals, and repeated responses that communicate what is acceptable.

Family issues that are handed down can significantly impact mental health. When children grow up in homes with high levels of conflict, emotional neglect, or inconsistent caregiving, they are more likely to experience anxiety, depression, and difficulty forming healthy relationships in adulthood.

This leads to a lens that can shape how individuals interpret the world, depending on their family environment. A lens built by unresolved family issues can distort perceptions of safety, trust, and belonging for years to come. But we have hope in God’s promises: “The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit.” (Psalm 34:18, NIV)

When Silence Becomes the Loudest Message

Avoiding difficult conversations is one of the most common family issues that affects mental health throughout generations. Families who develop unspoken rules about discussion tend to push certain topics under the surface. This influences behavior and emotional response in ways that feel confusing to those who are experiencing grief, addiction, mental illness, abuse, or simple disappointments.

When children grow up in environments where emotions are dismissed or minimized, they find it difficult to identify and express their own feelings as adults. This may lead them to experience emotional numbness, difficulty setting boundaries, or have feelings of intense shame when they experience strong emotions. Instead of protecting the family, the silence has created an isolation that leaves each generation to face its own challenges alone rather than together.

Christian counselors work with individuals who are beginning to recognize how family patterns of silence have shaped their mental health. This process encourages the understanding that vulnerability isn’t weakness and that naming pain doesn’t make it worse. Christian counselors emphasize that God’s design for family includes honesty, communication, and mutual support.

The concepts of identifying false beliefs and working with people are biblical. “Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to your neighbor, for we are all members of one body.” (Ephesians 4:25, NIV) This guides us and gives us hope in the process.

The Pressure to Repeat or Reject

Family issues that remain unaddressed will present difficult choices for future generations. These individuals can repeat the patterns they have witnessed or reject them entirely, but each choice will come with challenges. They find themselves repeating the patterns that create the same painful dynamics they have experienced. Rejecting everything about it can cause an individual to overreact and create new problems in their attempt to avoid old ones.

Adults who experience harsh discipline either replicate it with their own children or pivot to the opposite extreme, leaving them unable to set any boundaries. The underlying issue is the need to develop a thoughtful, intentional approach to family relationships based on health rather than rejection. However, neither of these approaches will address that underlying issue, so the healing process can’t begin.

The challenge of choosing to repeat or reject the patterns doesn’t just stop at parenting. Career choices, financial decisions, spiritual practices, and romantic relationships can become battlegrounds in which individuals either reenact or rebel against the family patterns of their past. Those who grew up in a home where faith was a tool of control often walk away from it, and others hold on tightly without ever examining what they actually believe.

Christian counselors help individuals navigate this terrain by exploring a path of healing and transformation, one that honors what was good while releasing what was harmful. This isn’t about assigning blame to the previous generation. It is about developing an honest understanding of where certain patterns came from and making a clear decision about where they will stop.

Creating New Patterns for Future Generations

To break generational cycles of family issues, individuals must be intentional, put in effort, invest time, practice self-awareness, and sometimes seek professional support. The starting point is recognizing that what feels normal isn’t necessarily healthy, and choosing a different path isn’t a betrayal of family.

Through this process, individuals will need to examine beliefs, behaviors, and emotional responses with honesty. They must learn to identify which patterns support well-being and which perpetuate harm.

Seeking professional help when family issues have created lasting impacts on mental health is important in processing pain, developing new skills, and building healthier patterns. This can feel unfamiliar at first, like trying to operate with an entirely different set of tools that includes emotional honesty, appropriate boundaries, and the capacity to give and receive support.

It is important to note that the work put into creating new patterns takes time. Patterns do not shift overnight after years of building. This is simply the nature of meaningful change, not an indication of failure.

The goal is to learn how to address the challenges that every family and generation faces. When family issues come into the light, they are met with appropriate support and discussed with compassion, and they no longer have the strength to dictate the future. Christian counselors work with families to create environments where mental health can flourish, patterns shift, and future generations develop tools for healing the pain that they inherited.

Isaiah reminds us how God does new things, even when we don’t expect it:

See, I am doing a new thing! Now it springs up; do you not perceive it? I am making a way in the wilderness and streams in the wasteland. – Isaiah 43:19, NIV

Learn to Break the Cycle of Family Issues

Family issues and mental health across generations have a connection that is both heavy and full of promise. It is sobering because it reveals how deeply past pain can reach into the present. It is hopeful because it shows that change is possible. With awareness, support, and intentional effort, families can create a new dynamic that promotes mental health rather than undermines it.

The cycle can be broken, and inheritance can change. Future generations do not have to receive a legacy of pain when they are given the tools to obtain the legacy of healing, resilience, and hope in Christ, transforming love. “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!” (2 Corinthians 5:17, NIV)

If family issues have shaped your mental health from past generations, you do not have to navigate the situation alone. Christian counselors are trained to help individuals understand the complex ways that family issues shape mental health and well-being.

item.title: Repressed Anger in Children: What Changes When Your Child Is Finally Heard and Validated
item.description:
As a parent, you know what it feels like to see your child upset but not know the full story. Sometimes your kid slams a door, or they just suddenly go quiet, and sometimes they just shrug and say, “I don’t care.” You know they’re not fine, but you don’t know how to reach them. Deep down, you know something is brewing.

What’s really happening in those instances is more than just attitude; most times, it’s repressed anger. Anger that is ignored in your child doesn’t just fade away; it festers inside, shaping how they think about themselves and how they respond to you and everyone else.

When that anger is finally heard and validated, something powerful happens. Your child begins to trust that their emotions matter, they stop pretending, they start opening up, and you begin to see the real person behind the silence or the fake smile.

The change that happens when you lean in and listen is bigger than calming a tantrum.

Common Situation Where Kids’ Anger Gets Buried

Repressed anger happens at so many points during a child’s day, not only during big fights. Sometimes kids can push down their emotions during simple activities like:

  • Homework arguments where your child stays silent but feels defeated inside
  • Food rules that spark frustration that they don’t dare express
  • Social settings where they smile but feel left out

All this sounds like it’s just part of ordinary life. After all, life isn’t always fair, isn’t it?

Well, for many kids, these are the times when validation matters most. When you notice the small things with the right mindset, you prevent bigger struggles later.

The Role of Sibling Dynamics in Repressed Anger

Anger doesn’t only build up between you and your child; it usually crops up in how they interact with their siblings. When one child feels overshadowed, unheard, or compared to a brother or sister, that frustration often gets buried instead of being expressed.

Repressed anger in your child may be seen in sarcasm, withdrawal during play, or even exaggerated politeness that hides resentment.

Parents sometimes miss these red flags because sibling rivalry is seen as normal. Yet when anger is consistently pushed down, it creates distance between siblings and teaches your child that their voice doesn’t matter in the family unit.

That’s why true validation changes the game. When you acknowledge the frustration your child feels toward a sibling, without judgment, you teach them that relationships can handle honesty. This not only helps your child release anger in healthier ways, but it also strengthens the bond between siblings over time.

Better ways to validate sibling‑related anger could include:

  • Letting each child explain their side without interruption
  • Avoiding comparisons like “your brother doesn’t complain.”
  • Encouraging shared problem‑solving instead of assigning blame

By validating anger related to children’s sibling dynamics, you’re showing your children that their emotions are safe to express, even in the closest relationships. This sets the stage for healthier communication patterns that last into adulthood.

This is an important lesson they can all carry into their adult lives with their own children later.

The Cost of Ignoring Their Anger

Think about the last time you felt dismissed. Maybe you were frustrated at work, and someone brushed you off with “don’t worry about it.” That didn’t make the frustration go away, did it? It probably made you feel small.

Kids feel the same way, maybe even worse, when their anger is ignored. When your child’s anger is brushed aside, they start believing their feelings don’t count. This can lead to:

  • Struggles with confidence
  • Difficulty being honest in friendships
  • A habit of pleasing others while ignoring their own needs

Ignoring anger doesn’t just stop a fight; it teaches your child to hide parts of themselves. It’s not just about their behavior; it’s about identity.

What Validation Really Means

Validation is not merely agreeing with everything your child says, but it’s more about acknowledging their feelings as real. When you say, “I hear that you’re upset,” or “I understand this feels unfair,” you’re telling your child their emotions are important.

Validation is like opening a door. It doesn’t solve the problem right away, but it makes your child feel safe enough to walk through and share more.

Why Parents Struggle with Validating Kids

To be honest, most parents worry that listening to anger will encourage disrespect. Or you may feel uncomfortable because you weren’t allowed to express anger as a kid yourself.

These might be real struggles for you, but they don’t have to define how you respond now.

When you avoid your child’s anger, you teach them to avoid conflict altogether. That might seem easier in the short term, but in the long run, it leaves them unprepared for relationships, school stress, and even faith questions.

What happens then? The toxic cycle continues, generation after generation.

How To Start Responding Better

There are many easy steps you can start trying out that go beyond the usual instinct to dole out advice or discipline, but help you connect with your child more deeply.

Ask questions that invite honesty: Instead of “Why are you angry?” try “What feels unfair to you right now?” This takes the focus from judgment to curiosity.

Use shared activities: Kids often talk more while playing a game, cooking, or walking. Create space where conversation feels natural instead of forced.

Teach them to notice body signals: Help your child recognize when their stomach tightens or their hands clench. This builds awareness before anger turns into silence.

Model your own process: Say more honest things about your own struggles, like, “I felt frustrated today, so I took a break before talking.” This shows them anger is manageable, not shameful.

Create a “safe word”: Agree on a word your child can use when they feel angry but don’t know how to explain it. This gives them a quick way to ask for support.

What Changes When Anger Is Validated

When a child consistently feels heard, and you validate your child’s anger, you’ll begin to notice changes like:

  • More honest conversations at home
  • They stop pretending. Your child no longer feels the need to fake calmness.
  • Less fear of conflict
  • Stronger emotional awareness
  • A deeper sense of trust between you and your child
  • They learn honesty. They begin to express what they feel without fear of rejection.
  • They grow stronger. By facing emotions directly, they build resilience for challenges ahead.

These changes don’t happen overnight, but they build over time.

The goal isn’t to control your child’s anger or make it disappear. The goal is to help them grow through it. Anger is a normal emotion, and when it’s validated, it becomes a tool for learning. Your child begins to see anger as something they can handle, not something they must hide.

This isn’t about fixing your child. It’s about giving them space to grow into who they already are.

Where To Find Professional Support for Repressed Anger

Sometimes, despite your best efforts, your child’s anger feels too complex to manage alone. That’s where counseling comes in. A professional counselor provides a safe space for your child to explore emotions without fear of judgment. Counseling also gives you tools to respond in ways that strengthen your relationship instead of weakening it.

Repressed anger in your child doesn’t have to define their story. When you hear and validate their emotions, you give them the gift of honesty, trust, and resilience. You also strengthen your bond in ways that last far beyond childhood.

If you’re ready to take the next step, consider reaching out to a professional counselor listed on this site. Call the numbers on the screen today and begin the process of helping your child turn repressed anger into growth, connection, and confidence.

item.title: 3 Types of Neurodiversity That Might Surprise You
item.description:
Types of neurodiversity may seem obvious if you’re speaking with someone who has non-verbal autism or maybe a child with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. You might recognize that someone with non-verbal autism communicates differently or that a child with ADHD struggles to maintain attention with competing priorities all at once.

However, understanding what neurodiversity is and isn’t helps everyone widen their view of what it means to be neurodivergent, how you can build accommodations into your everyday life, and how you can thrive no matter how your brain works.

Definition of Neurodiversity Versus Neurodivergent

Neurodiversity is the noun form of neurodivergent and simply refers to a state of having a brain that works differently from what is considered a norm or standard. Because it’s not a clinical definition, there are no specific criteria to meet; however, neurodiversity is used to classify someone whose brain operates uniquely compared to others.

Even two different people with the same diagnosis can have differently-wired brains, so comparing apples to apples (so to speak) isn’t going to result in a clear-cut definition. Neurotypical refers to someone whose brain operates in ways that are more culturally and socially accepted as standard. For example, someone who joins a group, introduces themselves, and starts to integrate into a group conversation might be considered neurotypical.

In contrast, someone who joins a group, stands off to the side, waits to be invited into the conversation, and still struggles to assert their opinion may show signs of a neurodiverse brain. Or they may just be shy until they’re comfortable in a new setting. It’s hard to tell at first glance, and it may not be visible whether someone is neurodiverse.

More Easily Identifiable Types of Neurodiversity

Conditions such as Down syndrome, ADHD, or Autism Spectrum Disorder have been widely publicized in the last three decades. Even if you haven’t met someone with these conditions, you’ve probably had some basic understanding of what the symptoms can look like.

It is important to note that not all conditions present the same in each individual, because no two brains are alike. All neurodiversity is based on a spectrum, and people cannot be boxed in based on how their brain works. The types of neurodiversity have been under a microscope recently because of an emphasis on busting myths and shifting to more accepting language and workplace environments.

For example, one myth says that someone who is “special education” or “disabled” cannot learn like others. However, the more accurate term, neurodiverse learners, actually means these children or adults are just as capable as others. Still, their brains have developed differently, so they may not process the information in the same way that neurotypical brains do.

Does it mean that neurodiverse learners are dumb or less likely to succeed? No, in fact, quite the opposite. Studies show that neurodiversity can be a super-strength because a brain that developed differently or processes information differently has strengths that a neurotypically developing brain may not.

3 Types of Neurodiversity You May Not Know About

While we may think we know about ADHD or Autism Spectrum Disorder, there are likely aspects of each that many are unaware of. Here are three aspects of neurodiversity that could surprise you.

1. ADHD learners can focus for long periods of time on certain tasks or pursuits

A neurotypical brain may be able to focus for sustained periods of time, synthesize and go between various forms of information intermittently without any issues, and transition from task to task easily. However, someone with ADHD may struggle with these processes. The underlying cause, though, isn’t a lack of attention, as the name implies.

Instead, many people with ADHD can focus for extended periods of time if the task is a strength, such as creative pursuits. Many highly creative people — artists, songwriters and musicians, authors, and actors — are diagnosed with ADHD, and their ability to sustain focus on their artistic pursuits helps them in their chosen career field.

So, why does the name refer to attention deficit?

When the neurodevelopmental condition that we now know as ADHD was identified, it was considered a deficit in someone’s attention span. Much of the early research was from children with the condition, who tended to show signs of impulsivity. However, just like not everyone strong in computational skills enjoys algebra, not everyone with ADHD is impulsive.

Instead of viewing neurodeficits, we now recognize that all brains are different, which is where the term neurodiverse comes from.

Did you know that a person with inattentive ADHD can sustain focus for long periods of time without regard for other pursuits? This may explain why artists like Mary-Jo Lough can create intricate paintings for hours. In an interview for the Arts to Hearts Project, Lough said that her process of making the art is exhibited in the painting itself, layered over a sustained period of time.

She said, “After several layers, I gradually see a connected movement between the shapes and marks. This is when I begin to refine, incorporating deliberate details, lines, patterns, and textures. This process of building up and breaking down mirrors how my mind works, constantly shifting and reordering thoughts, noticing connections and patterns until they form a cohesive whole. The ability to hyperfocus during these moments allows me to dive deep into the details, ensuring every aspect of the piece resonates with my vision.” (Lough)

Hyperfocus is a strength if you’re an actor learning lines for a script, on a movie set for 14-16 hours a day. It’s also a strength if you are a designer, crafting fashions on a laptop and then taking them from the design phase to the material that will one day adorn the person who buys them.

2. Dyslexia may make you a more creative problem solver

Many people think that there’s simply one type of dyslexia and that it means you can’t read or that letters jump around on the page. This is a misnomer because there are also subcategories of dyslexia, some of which include phonological, surface, and rapid naming.

According to the International Dyslexia Association, dyslexia is “a specific learning disability characterized by difficulties in word reading and/or spelling that involve accuracy, speed, or both and vary depending on the orthography. These difficulties occur along a continuum of severity and persist even with instruction that is effective for the individual’s peers. The causes of dyslexia are complex and involve combinations of genetic, neurobiological, and environmental influences that interact throughout development.” (International Dyslexia Association)

While dyslexia definitely presents challenges for some with skills like processing language, reading pace, writing, or decoding sounds, it isn’t insurmountable. Because of these challenges, a more positive outlook suggests that dyslexic people find ways around their obstacles.

Dyslexic people often think outside the box and are able to visualize 3-D elements in ways that neurotypical learners can’t. They can solve problems, recognizing solutions that aren’t linear in nature or wouldn’t be based on categorization of information attributed to research or reading.

Multisensory learning has proven highly successful with people who have dyslexia because it teaches concepts that are processed through more than one sense. This makes it more likely that dyslexic people will use a variety of senses to solve challenges in the workplace or in their everyday life, rather than simply focusing on one or two senses.

3. Autism Spectrum Disorder may mean you excel in finding patterns, identifying non-language-based sequencing, or code-breaking

Why would types of neurodiversity focus on strengths based on shape and pattern vs. strengths based on language acquisition? One reason is that some people’s brains are better at recognizing recurring patterns, odd patterns that don’t fit a paradigm, or even idiosyncrasies in shapes and structures.

If you’re autistic, some of these skills could be where you excel, even if communicative behavior is a challenge or complex hidden social cues tax your brain. Sadly, social cues are often prized as cultural strengths. Still, the need for strong nonverbal reasoning skills, such as puzzles, logic sequences, and code-breaking, is becoming dominant in the career landscape.

Companies are recognizing that they need the strengths of all neurodiverse people, including autistic ones. These are people who can look at patterns and identify the ones that aren’t working, and excel at combining complex tables or designing unique elements of a product. While types of neurodiversity abound because brain wiring is multifaceted, societal perspectives of neurodiverse learners are shifting.

Cultural adaptations and decades-long myths mean we still have a long way to go, which means you may be struggling with self-esteem because of how you’ve been labeled or perceived in the past. If you are a neurodiverse thinker and are struggling, our offices are equipped to help.

Seeking out a psychologist or counselor who can guide you to view yourself through a strengths-based lens may be what gives you the mindset you need to see yourself as successful and thriving. Reach out to this office to learn more about the support services offered.

item.title: 5 Things You Need to Know About Intrusive Thoughts
item.description:
At some point, everyone has had an unexpected thought that whispers something like, “Did I switch the stove off after breakfast this morning?” You might easily dismiss a thought like this, or you might text a roommate or spouse, asking them to make sure that the stove is off if they are home.

For people without OCD, intrusive thoughts are like little stabs of panic that come out of nowhere and fade as fast as they appeared. They can even be helpful prompts, ensuring that they double-check important details that would otherwise be forgotten.

By contrast, people with OCD are tortured by intrusive thoughts, and the thoughts don’t lead to anything that could be considered helpful. They are more than little stabs of panic; they are relentless, repetitive, exhausting, and they often feel impossible to ignore.

Intrusive thoughts are a symptom of OCD that fuels obsessive behavior and results in compulsive behavior. The repeating anxious thought that you forgot to switch the stove off before you left home might result in you having to check that all appliances in the home are off multiple times before you feel safe enough to leave the house.

In this case, the intrusive thoughts are not helpful because they cause untold amounts of anxiety and have resulted in you developing a compulsive ritual.

Five Things to Know About Intrusive Thoughts

Sometimes people without OCD have disturbing intrusive thoughts, like having an urge to make a noise at a funeral, or wondering what it would feel like to jump off the precipice they are standing on. Thoughts of violence or unusual behavior like this are your brain’s way of preparing you for every outcome in the situation, no matter how unlikely.

Your brain is prompting you to be prepared should something unexpected happen. Even when the thought is dark or disturbing in nature, it is never compelling enough to be acted upon, and most people dismiss these intrusive thoughts with a laugh to themselves.

OCD intrusive thoughts, however, are relentless, and the people who experience them feel as if they cannot be dismissed except by actively responding to them.

These intrusive thoughts frequently center around topics like harm and violence to self or others, taboo or sexually provocative ideas, anxiety around disease and contamination, stress over asymmetry or imbalances, fear of offending God or others with sinful behavior, and intrusive thoughts around responsibility and duty.

When you have a thought playing on an endless loop in your mind, and when it is shocking or controversial in nature, you will be anxious, ashamed, and afraid of the potential consequences of even having that thought.

The more you understand about intrusive thoughts and OCD, the better you can help yourself and others. You are not a bad person for having any of the intrusive thoughts you have, and you are also not beyond help.

Here are five things you need to know about intrusive thoughts:

Sometimes intrusive thoughts sound like suggestions and prompts

Intrusive thoughts frequently sound like what–if scenarios, such as, “What if I don’t wash my hands before eating?” or “What if I punched my child in the head right now?” Sometimes, though, intrusive thoughts sound more like prompts or suggestions to do these things. An urge to refrain from washing your hands does not sound as serious as an urge to injure your child, but to the person with OCD, both thoughts feel equally intense and shameful.

Intrusive thoughts are unwanted

Every thought that comes into our heads feels as if it is a part of us. Our thoughts, particularly when they are urges or prompts, feel as if they come from our personal values or beliefs. This is not the case with intrusive thoughts.

Intrusive thoughts are ego-dystonic, which means they do not come from your values or character. In fact, intrusive thoughts challenge and clash with your values and character. This is why they feel exhausting and disturbing to face. They are opposed to who you are as a person. It is like wrestling with an enemy inside your brain.

Intrusive thoughts are irrational

If you have OCD, you will naturally over-interpret every thought you have. If you try to rationalize every intrusive thought, you will come to some disturbing conclusions about yourself, but they are conclusions without any basis.

For example, if you have an intrusive thought urging you to curse God or to blaspheme the Holy Spirit, you might conclude that you are sinful and that you must work to regain your purity. Just as intrusive thoughts do not reflect your character or values, they are also irrational most of the time.

On some level, you might know that your intrusive thoughts are irrational. For example, if you checked that the stove was off before leaving home, it is irrational to worry that it might still be on, somehow. This is what leads people to develop checking rituals.’

They check while counting the number of times they have checked, and this ritual becomes their first line of defense against the irrational, intrusive thoughts. They can at least tell themselves that they have checked it multiple times and that they can be sure.

Intrusive thoughts do not define you

It can be helpful to think of thoughts as visitors, and this is especially true for intrusive thoughts. Your thoughts do not always originate in your own brain. They are sometimes a product of your environment, of your mental state, or, in the case of OCD and intrusive thoughts, they are a product of extreme anxiety.

Intrusive thoughts are like a home invasion. They come from outside of you, they strong-arm their way into your mind while holding you hostage, and they assault your values. Intrusive thoughts can be as traumatizing as this home invasion analogy. Still, the important thing to remember is that these thoughts and disturbing prompts do not reflect your morals or values, and they do not define your character.

You are not helpless in dealing with intrusive thoughts

As debilitating and exhausting as it is to deal with OCD and intrusive thoughts, you are not beyond help. There are a few effective forms of therapy for OCD, and you can begin to deal with intrusive thoughts on your own, as they appear. The trick is not to try to eliminate these thoughts, but to change your relationship with them.

Firstly, name the thought as a product of OCD. When you can identify and name an intrusive thought for what it is, it begins to lose its ability to affect you so intensely. Intrusive thoughts are common, frequent, and distressing. When you begin to name them as a symptom of OCD, though, they become separated from your identity.

Secondly, stop doing the compulsions associated with the intrusive thoughts. Intrusive thoughts make you anxious, and one of your most trusted ways of dealing with that anxiety is to perform some repetitive action. You might worry about contracting a disease after touching a trash can, for example, and your trusted way of dealing with that worry is to wash your hands multiple times until the panic subsides.

These rituals and repetitive actions tell your brain that the only effective way to deal with the anxiety and intrusive thoughts is to perform that certain action. This keeps you locked into the cycle of OCD, from intrusive thought to compulsive action. When you get therapy for OCD, you will begin facing and dealing with these compulsive behaviors and learning that it is safe to stop doing them.

Next Steps

OCD isn’t easy to deal with alone. If you don’t know where to find help, consider meeting with a counselor to discuss your experience. We host an online catalog of counselors where you might find someone suitable to meet with, or you could speak with our reception team. You don’t have to struggle alone anymore. Reach out today.

item.title: Can You Heal from Church Trauma?
item.description:
One of the greatest betrayals is when someone who is supposed to be universally and inherently on your side causes you harm. This type of double-cross has caused great damage throughout history. Look at the way Judas betrayed Christ, or how children of abusive parents grow up with a lion’s share of trauma they must deal with. People still experience this today, even in settings like the church.

Different Types of Trauma

This harmful betrayal is not confined to biblical times or hidden behind closed doors. It can also happen in the larger Christian church body. The church is supposed to be a holy place, filled with Christ-followers. And while this is the ideal and is the case in many healthy congregations, it’s not universally true.

The reality is that the church is a place filled with fallible people, often trying their best. Sometimes they make mistakes. Sometimes they inadvertently hurt each other. And sometimes the church has been infiltrated with sinister people who use the name of Christ to give them authority to do hurtful things.

Abuse in the Church

Some church trauma goes beyond the hurtful to abuse, and in some extreme cases, it’s also criminal. Sexual assault, grooming, spiritual coercion, and the misuse of power by leaders who hide behind their position are all serious violations. These violations can happen even in a church context.

When things like this happen in the church, the damage is tied to a spiritual context. There is something uniquely disorienting about being harmed in a place that is supposed to be a holy refuge. When a leader uses Scripture and the name of God to manipulate and abuse you, it not only affects you emotionally and mentally but can cause significant spiritual damage as well.

Abuse is never justified, even by faith or religious authority. It shouldn’t be tolerated because of tradition or dismissed because of the Christian mandate of forgiveness taken out of context. Abuse done in a church context is explicitly wrong.

If you’ve experienced any type of abuse or exploitation within a church setting, rest assured that it was not your fault, nor was it something you caused. No matter what you did or wore, the responsibility falls entirely on the person who harmed you and anyone who enabled them.

Reporting criminal abuse to the proper authorities is a necessary act of justice that protects both your own safety and the safety of the entire community. Sadly, when abuse happens within the church, leaders sometimes forgo reporting to the authorities.

Less Obvious Harm

Not all church trauma comes from extreme and clearly defined abuse. Sometimes, church trauma is a culmination of a series of repeated negative or careless experiences that slowly push someone out the stained-glass door.

While not abuse, the feeling of being consistently left out of the inner circle can also create a negative association with church. Conversations that stop when you walk into a room and invitations that never come can send the message that you’re not accepted. Favoritism is also damaging to church bodies. When certain people are celebrated, and cliques form within the church, the place of community can start feeling suspiciously similar to a high school cafeteria.

Other times, it is connected to things like serving. While we are called to serve within the church, some churches abuse that power. Even if you were pressured into serving constantly, especially when you see others not contributing, it can cause you to feel used and underappreciated.

If you’ve been a victim of serious trauma at the hands of someone who professed Christianity or was in a Christian authority over you, you know how deeply that betrayal cuts. Even if what caused your church trauma wasn’t illegal or even immoral, it can still leave a scar. Whether your church trauma was truly a result of abuse or just carelessness, the result can be a broken spirit and maybe even a broken relationship with God.

The Aftermath of Abuse

The unfortunate result of abuse in the church is often church trauma. It’s the law of cause and effect in action. If you are harmed by someone who wears the label of Christianity, you are going to associate them and their professed belief with the negative impact it left on you.

Unfortunately, that impact often ripples beyond the initial incident. It can create a deep-seated mistrust toward anything that resembles organized religion. This mistrust can compel people to turn to other non-Christian spiritual beliefs or to develop a disdain for anything associated with Christianity. This change in behavior and belief can carry on throughout a lifetime.

If you’ve been wronged by the church or someone in Christian authority, it might change the way you raise your children. While you might have grown up in the church, your church-related trauma now prevents you from raising your own children within an organized church body.

Sometimes a negative church experience can even impact your relationship with God. It can be difficult to separate what people do in the name of Christ from Christ Himself, especially on an emotional level.

Can you heal?

The short answer is yes, you can overcome church trauma and learn to trust God and His people again. While God can heal and deliver you from the trauma of your past, your healing may require you to invest some time and effort.

Find the truth

To fully heal from church trauma, you need to recognize that the people who represented Christ to you were, in those moments, acting in direct opposition to His nature. Separating the mistakes and actions of a specific person or group from Christ Himself isn’t always easy, especially when those lines were blurred for a long time.

When you do separate the two, you will often find that God is different than how He has been represented. He, too, was wronged by their actions, and while He was innocent, His name and reputation got tarnished in the process.

Get to know Christ

Educate yourself on the nature of Christ. Read the Bible, listen to worship music, and talk with Bible-believing friends about God’s love and nature. By educating yourself, you will discover that Christ brings freedom, love, and grace. You will find that He heals, restores, and loves in a way that is not humanly possible.

Forgive

Depending on the complexity, severity, and duration of your trauma, forgiveness might be difficult. But you don’t have to do it alone. Christ forgave those who murdered Him, and He will help you forgive those who have harmed you, too.

Forgiveness is not justifying their action, but it takes the power away from it and them. When you live in a state of unforgiveness, you are perpetually giving power to the act and the people who have harmed you. But when you release forgiveness, not through your own strength, but in the name of Jesus, you are removing the power your trauma holds over you.

This doesn’t mean that those responsible for your trauma shouldn’t be held accountable for their action. It means that you are making the deliberate decision not to let their actions dictate the rest of your life.

It’s also important to realize that your anger is a righteous response to injustice and that true biblical forgiveness never requires you to remain in a relationship with those who use Scripture as a tool of control or to silence you.

Seek support

Church trauma affects emotional, mental, and relational health, and these are areas that can benefit from professional support.

Working with a licensed Christian therapist can give you the opportunity to fully communicate and understand the experiences that formed your church trauma. It allows you to grieve what was lost and rebuild not only your sense of self, but your relationship with God.

If you’ve been victimized by someone who professed the name of Christ, know that they don’t speak for Him. God loves you unconditionally. He does not approve of abusive behavior, and He wants to heal you. He can help you forgive and to move on to find a body of believers who will help restore true fellowship.

People are fallible and will disappoint you. God is unwavering in His constant love and wants to meet you right where you are. If you have church-related trauma, consider what it might look like to invite God and a professional mental health specialist into the healing process.

Call and schedule an appointment with Joseph. I would be grateful for the opportunity to walk alongside you in this healing journey.

item.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and the Hidden Cost of Growing Up in a Conflict-Free Home
item.description:
It may seem strange to say that quiet households aren’t necessarily healthy. Homes where there are no arguments between the parents, no slamming doors, and no visible discord are often depicted as the perfect home environment. But there are times that this perfect environment feels off. There’s an unnamed uneasiness, lingering in the shadows. Adverse childhood experiences aren’t just a product of loud and volatile environments.

These experiences often have roots embedded in homes where there was no conflict. In these homes, the silence itself has become the message. It’s important to pay attention to this as Scripture is clear about how to raise children:

“Train up a child in the way he should go, even when he is old he will not depart from it.” Proverbs 22:6, NASB 1995

Adverse Childhood Experiences in the Spaces Between the Words

Society commonly associates adverse childhood experiences with obvious harm such as abuse, neglect, or a household shaped by addiction or violence. But the definition reaches far beyond those familiar categories.

Other areas connected to adverse childhood experiences are emotional unavailability, chronically unresolved dynamics, or emotional environments that children absorb before they have a language to describe them. When conflict is permanently suppressed within a home, a different set of messages is sent.

Children are more perceptive than parents give them credit for. They notice when there is a proverbial elephant in the room that no one is talking about. The weight of unspoken disagreements and a cool distance between their parents are things that children can pick up on, even though no words have been spoken. What they see, and what they don’t see, is quietly shaping the way they understand the dynamics of relationships and how they should work.

When conflict is avoided, children often grow up believing that any form of disagreement is unsafe. This leaves them navigating adulthood without knowing how to have hard conversations in a way that doesn’t end in shutting down or walking away. This results in the lesson that conflict must be avoided at all costs rather than worked through. This is a lesson that most people do not recognize until adulthood.

How Adverse Childhood Experiences Shape Emotional Development

The emotional map that children use to navigate their feelings, relationships, and sense of self stems from the emotional landscape they grow up in. Christian counselors emphasize that individuals who present with anxiety, emotional avoidance, or difficulty sustaining a close relationship can trace those patterns back to early home environments.

These environments were not always chaotic, but they did lack emotional honesty. A conflict-free home doesn’t mean it is automatically healthy. The difference between these two types of homes matters in how a child’s emotional development happens.

Adults who were raised in households where healthy disagreement was never modeled often develop a heightened sensitivity to perceived social threats. These adults can read the room and learn to manage the emotions of those around them, quietly disappearing into whatever version of themselves fits the situation.

This leads to an internal fracture that masks a persistent, ongoing dilemma of not knowing whether their own feelings are acceptable. These adults spend many years managing others instead of realizing they have never learned to manage themselves. Emotional suppression in the home can give way to lasting difficulties in emotional regulation, self-worth, and relational intimacy. The soul will carry what the mind cannot yet fully process.

Faith, Healing, and the Permission to Feel

Scripture gives us a profound gift centered on the permission to feel emotions. The book of Psalms is a testament that God does not require positive feelings all the time. Grief, frustration, lament, and longing are woven throughout the biblical narrative from Genesis to Revelation. Adults who grapple with the residue of a childhood spent trying to understand emotional silence can understand the transformation of this biblical narrative.

God created us and does not demand that we hide our feelings; he invites them. He welcomes our open, honest feelings so He can comfort us and work in us.

Christian counselors understand that the healing process from early relational wounds is not a straight line. The adult will be required to learn how to identify emotions that were never given names or sit with discomfort that was once suppressed. They will need to understand how to rebuild a sense of what a safe connection feels and looks like.

These things can be found when faith serves as a foundation. This leads to confidence that God is present in the slow, hard process of becoming whole. This principle is the basis for genuine and lasting change.

The spiritual aspect of this process is significant in helping adults identify how they have internalized a distorted image of God as a result of growing up in conflict-avoidant homes. It removes the lens that says God is emotionally unavailable and requires composed compliance instead of a relationship. Scripture dismantles this image and offers one that says God draws near in the places we keep most guarded.

“Do not fear, for I am with you; Do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you, I will also help you, I will also uphold you with My righteous right hand.” – Isaiah 41:10, NASB

Support for What You Could Not Name

One of the most complex dynamics adults experience is difficulty identifying what is wrong. They have no recollection of a dramatic event or of any identifiable wound. But they know that they have lingering effects in relationships and emotional availability.

They noticed that their sense of self was affected, and Christian counselors can provide the essential help needed to understand what happened. The result will be healing that is possible and worth pursuing.

When adults are willing to seek support, they are choosing to take an honest look at what they absorbed in childhood. It doesn’t mean they need to assign blame, but rather to bring the unnamed experiences into the light for addressing.

This will illuminate a connection between early emotional environments and their current relational patterns, allowing them to relax. They find they no longer need to maintain an impossible balancing act and can move forward with the healing that comes from naming the struggle.

Faith is a reminder that we are not required to carry these struggles alone. We were not designed to carry the burdens alone. Through community and honest conversations, we find that it is not weakness but rather reinforcement that will create a flourishing lifestyle based on the life that Scripture points to. We are reminded of God’s faithfulness to care for us in Psalm 147: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NASB)

Moving Toward Wholeness

It may not look like an issue that causes a struggle, but homes without healthy conflict create a specific kind of loss. It is a loss that goes unnamed and unknown for years. The face of a quiet adverse childhood experience is not easy to recognize, yet it is important to address. It is not an easy thing to name what happened in relation to adverse childhood experiences, but it is where everything shifts.

We don’t surprise God with our baggage. There is no distance from the layers of work that come with healing from what we absorbed before we could speak the words. Our journey toward wholeness doesn’t require having everything figured out. It only asks that we be willing to start and trust that we are not on the road alone. God is faithful to work things out for His good.

“And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.” – Romans 8:28, NASB

Can you identify with any of this information? If so, please do not hesitate to contact the office and speak with the reception team. They can get you set up with an appointment to meet with the right counselor and start your journey to heal the wounds that have gone unnamed.
